text: Chapter 3 has given you every individual and group role a governance program needs. This closing lesson covers the one role that determines whether any of the others actually stick: executive sponsorship.

Industry research on governance program failure returns to the same finding again and again: a lack of sustained executive sponsorship is one of the most common reasons programs fail. Owners and stewards only carry real authority when someone senior enough to matter is visibly backing their role.

A real sponsor isn't a figurehead who signs off once. The job has four ongoing parts: aligning governance with business strategy so it solves problems people actually care about, securing real budget and time, modeling the behavior in the rooms where priorities get set, and breaking ties at the top when the governance committee itself can't resolve something.

Sponsorship usually doesn't disappear in one dramatic moment — it erodes quietly. Watch for the signs: a name on a slide who's never attended a meeting, governance work that always loses to other priorities without pushback, or nobody on the team being able to say who the sponsor actually is.
Roles, committees, RACI, and sponsorship — that's the complete structure Chapter 3 set out to build. Next chapter covers what that structure actually produces: policies and standards. See you there.
